div.p: Most statistics state that disabled people constitute approximately 20% of the world population; therefore, webmasters should consider this part of the world population when they design and implement their websites by following the web content accessibility guidelines. This paper aims to explore the relationships between web accessibility, web traffic (web), and university rankings using the metrics of 27 Jordanian university websites as a case study. Objective evaluations on the web accessibility, web traffic (website popularity), and university rankings of 27 Jordanian university websites are conducted using a number of online tools. An extensive analysis of the tool outputs is presented, and the relationships of these tool outputs are explored. This study represents a longitudinal overview of the accessibility of Jordanian university websites and re-explores the different relationships between web accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings, as well as the differences between the accessibility of private and public Jordanian universities. This paper explores the relationships between three parameters: accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings. Therefore, its scope is larger than earlier publications.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The World Wide Web (WWW) has witnessed the development of many new technologies to present information since its onset. The concept of WWW is different from the concept of cloud computing, where the services in cloud computing include providing shared computing resources across the internet to different machines (Do and Hussain, 2013). The scope of this study does not include any requirements validation of cloud systems (Moscato, 2015). The evolution of the WWW should involve providing web accessibility to disabled people. In addition to adopting web content accessibility guidelines (WCAG) in their websites, therefore, webmasters should ensure that their websites could accommodate new devices (smartphones, tablets, and computers regardless of their screen size) to benefit disabled internet users who use their websites. These websites are becoming more complex; hence, their compliance with WCAG is becoming more difficult. The first version of WCAG (WCAG 1.0) was released in 1999 and consists of 14 guidelines; each guideline is subdivided into checkpoints. The total number of these checkpoints is 65, and each checkpoint has three priority levels (Priority 1, Level A conformance; Priority 2, Level AA conformance; and Priority 3, Level AAA conformance). The second version of WCAG (WCAG 2.0) was released in 2008, and it consists of 12 guidelines and success criteria organised around four principles. Each success criterion describes specifically what must be achieved to conform to the guideline to which it belongs. The total number of success criteria in this version is 61. Websites that comply with these necessary guidelines ensure an accessible web environment. Manual evaluation is thought to be the most suitable choice to assess accessibility, but it is no more a feasible choice because the size of many websites is becoming unmanageable. In this approach, a specialised team is recruited to conduct a manual evaluation. Funds need to be allocated to the team, and waiting for their results takes time. Automatic accessibility evaluation tools are the most desirable choice because many of these tools are free and do not need a long waiting period for the results. These automatic online accessibility evaluation tools can help to correct accessibility errors. They also widely differ in their capabilities. These errors are different from those faults of different software systems (Munawar and Ward, 2011). However, many checkpoints can be manually tested only; hence, using these tools will not guarantee web accessibility. Evaluations with disabled internet users should be conducted to identify specific problems. Webmasters who plan to build accessible websites should use these evaluation tools during the web development life cycle.

WebAIM's web accessibility versatile evaluator (WAVE) (http://wave.webaim.org/) uses an application program interface and is one of the most satisfactory free online tools for testing whether web pages are accessible to blind people. The WAVE tool was originally developed and sponsored by the Temple University Institute on Disabilities in Pennsylvania. The WAVE tool analyses the web page under consideration automatically and embeds icons and indicators. The WAVE tool also generates graphical and readable output for visually capable evaluators. WAVE enables web developers to identify most accessibility problems (accessibility violations) on their web pages. Red icons indicate accessibility errors, yellow icons indicate alerts or possible accessibility error, green icons indicate features, blue icons indicate structural or semantic elements, and purple icons indicate the use of HTML 5 structural elements or ARIA roles, states, or properties. Black icons indicate colour contrast errors according to WCAG guidelines. The WAVE tool is a quick and efficient way to identify many accessibility problems and features of the websites, and is thus used in the present study. WebAIM's WAVE accessibility reporting page does not provide its evaluation report in terms of 'pass' or 'fail'. Two additional free online tools are used to assess accessibility: AccessMonitor (http://www.acessibilidade.gov.pt/accessmonitor/) and the European Internet Inclusion Initiative (EIII) Page Checker (http://checkers.eiii.eu/). Accessible websites enable normal and disabled people to visit them; consequently, the number of visitors (web traffic/website popularity) will increase, which may have a positive effect on the rank of university websites.

The higher education sector plays an essential role in building a generation of thinkers in different fields of science, technology, and humanities. Therefore, many countries, including developing countries, realise the role that science can play in driving economic development. National governments should invest in their science base to secure economic prosperity even in a period of economic turbulence. Hence, many national governments have presented a number of reforms in education and invested in infrastructure and projects designed to create knowledgebased economies. Education reforms take place when governments recognise that technology and innovation are key elements to achieve long-term economic and social development. Thus, expenditure on research and development is increased significantly by governments that have realised the significance of this type of investment in the past few years. In most cases, increased investment in research and development leads to increased university rankings. A number of magazines, universities, newspapers, websites, and governments conduct the ranking assessment of different higher education establishments worldwide. Therefore, many global rankings of colleges and universities exist; these rankings are different because of the difference in the algorithms that were used for ranking. In the present study, Jordan is selected because it lies in the middle of the list of Arab countries by population (Wikipedia 2016). In addition, according to Elgohary (2008), Jordanian universities constitute 40% of the top 10 Arab universities. To identify the ranks of 27 Jordanian universities, the present study is based on the Webometrics Ranking of World Universities published by Cybermetrics Lab because it is the only comprehensive university ranking that includes the rank of the 27 Jordanian universities.

Some specialists define web traffic as the number of visitors to a website; others define it as the amount of data sent and received by internet users to a website, excluding the traffic generated by web crawlers. Generally, the number of visitors to a website is not distributed equally on its web pages. Hence, the web traffic to each website is monitored by the website owner to identify popular web pages and links. Many free tools can be used to monitor website traffic, such as Google Analytics and Alexa.com. Alexa.com is used in this study to identify the ranks of 27 Jordanian university websites on the national and world levels; the national rank is used to identify its relationships to accessibility and university rankings.

This paper aims to explore the homepages of 27 Jordanian websites to determine their accessibility barriers (accessibility violations) and rank these websites according to their web traffic, web accessibility scores, and university rankings.

Websites that comply with WCAG are called accessible websites to people with disabilities. This study also aims to rediscover whether any relationship exists between accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings. Moreover, this study tests different hypotheses about the relationships between accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings. Although prior studies such as Lilly et al. (1999), Schmetzke (2001) and Kane et al. (2007) show no significant correlation between the ranks of the universities and their accessibilities, we conduct this study to rediscover these relationships, and found no significant correlations between the ranks of the universities and their accessibilities. Kendall's tau and Spearman's (rho) rank correlation coefficients are used to determine the relationships between accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings. The scope of this paper is larger than scope or earlier studies, wince it explores the relationships between three parameters: accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings.

The remaining parts of this paper are organised as follows: Section 2 presents a summary of a number of studies related to exploring the relationships between web accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings. Section 3 presents the methodology adopted in this study. Section 4 discusses the statistical methods. Section 5 presents the conclusions and future plans to improve this study.

div.head: Literature review
div.p: The relationship between accessibility and popularity of websites is presented by a number of studies, one of which is conducted by Lilly et al. (1999). Those authors include the library home web pages of Yahoo!'s list of the '100 Most Wired Colleges' in their study; they also use Bobby tool to analyse the accessibility of the web pages' understudy. The Bobby tool identifies 40 library homepages as accessible, and the study concludes that no relationship exists between accessibility and popularity. Our new study concludes that a negative relationship is present between accessibility and web traffic. In addition, Schmetzke (2001) uses the US News and World Report to determine the library home web pages of the top 24 schools of library and information science in the U.S. He discovered that 4 out of the 24 library websites are 100% accessible and that no relationship exists between accessibility and popularity. Hackett et al. (2004) use the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine to select a random sample of websites from 1997 to 2002. Their sample consists of 240 websites that are distributed equally within those six years. They aim to study the effects of technology on accessibility, and they conclude that the adoption of new technologies in web pages increase their complexities, thereby increasing accessibility barriers.

The accessibilities of university websites are studied by many authors because these institutions should offer knowledge indiscriminately to all people whether they are disabled or not. One of these studies is conducted by Kane et al. (2007), which included a multi-method analysis of the homepages of the top 100 universities in the world; Kane et al. (2007) consider the homepage as a representative of each university's website, which is a debatable issue. These homepages are analysed for their compliance with accessibility standards, choice of language, image accessibility, text-only content, and quality of web accessibility statements. The effects of language, geographic location, public funding status, and university ranking on university's level of web accessibility are also studied in their study. They conclude that a significant geographical variation exists in the website accessibility of these 100 universities in addition to the accessibility errors; many of those websites lack accessibility policies or documentation. Few homepages approach full accessibility, specifically those in English-speaking countries, such as the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia. The accessibility of the homepage of each public Portuguese university is examined by Espadinha et al. (2011); they used two recommended online tools, namely eXaminator and HERA, by the Portuguese government to measure the conformance of the websites under study with WCAG checkpoints and detect errors. They conclude that only 12.5% of these websites are accessible. Comeaux et al. (2007) investigate the websites of 56 American Library Association-accredited library schools. They use manual and automatic evaluation of these websites. Bobby 3.1.1 tool is used to evaluate the accessibilities of these sites automatically. Their results indicate an improvement in accessibility, but the used tool could not detect any Bobby-detectable errors in 50%-60% of the 56 websites under study. They conclude that Canadian websites are more accessible than US websites, and a relationship exists between popularity and accessibility. They also test the accessibility of each of the 56 websites of North American academic libraries (Comeaux et al., 2013). Furthermore, they test the relationship between table-and CSS-based designs and accessibility, and conclude that a larger sample should be used to determine the effect of these designs on accessibility.

Two studies by Lopes and Carriço (2010) and Lopes et al. (2010) show high variability on the accessibility level of different web pages, and the low percentage of these web pages gains high accessibility levels. Furthermore, these two studies conclude that a correlation exists between accessibility and complexity. Kaur et al. (2014) investigate the accessibilities of bank websites in India and find that all bank websites in India have accessibility barriers; their accessibility evaluation reveals no difference among the (private and public) bank websites in India. They also discover a positive correlation between complexity and importance, and a negative significant correlation between complexity and popularity. In addition, they conclude that no significant relation exists between accessibility from one side and complexity, importance, and popularity from the other side. Buenadicha et al. (2001) propose a new web assessment index (WAI); their index is based on four key quality factors (accessibility, speed, navigability, and website content) that are essential to determine the quality of a website. They use their index to evaluate the websites of all Spanish universities and determine each of their score (based on a total of 100 points). Buenadicha et al. (2001) present a high correlation between site popularity and university size (number of students). A similar study by Gonzalez et al. (2004) proposes the WAI, which is based on the same four key factors presented by Buenadicha et al. (2001); these authors show a high correlation value between site popularity and firm size. Furthermore, Zeng (2004) concludes that a significant relationship exists between WAB score and Alexa traffic ranking in his Ph.D. thesis; however, no statistically significant relationship is observed between WAB and PageRank scores.

Typically, the empirical analysis of the relationship between website ranking and accessibility score involves a bivariate correlation analysis; such analysis is conducted by Kamoun et al. (2014) using 21 websites that are affiliated with the Dubai e-government. They conclude that a weak correlation exists between e-government website ranking and their web accessibility scores.

The relationship between accessibility and complexity is also explored by Hackett et al. (2004); they discover that governmental websites remain accessible and that using new technologies within web pages lead to an increased complexity, thereby increasing the number of accessibility barriers.

Many studies explore the correlation between the accessibility scores of (URLs/websites) and other metrics, such as web rank and complexity. Freire et al. (2008) study the correlation between different web accessibility metrics and also present a good survey of recent progress in this area of study.

Accessibility is considered a subset of usability by some experts in this field, whereas others consider usability a subset of accessibility. Therefore, a number of studies were conducted to show the relation between accessibility and usability. Petrie et al. (2007) show an overlap in the problems that face both disabled and non-disabled people; however, they fail to find any relationship between the ratings of the participants, researchers, and usability guidelines regardless of whether they are disabled or not. They conclude that accessibility problems are not a complete subset of usability problems and that usability problems are not a complete subset of accessibility problems. Sullivan et al. (2000) also conclude a weak correlation between content accessibility and overall usability.

div.head: Methodology
div.p: This section is divided into three subsections. The first subsection presents the selection of websites used in this study, the second subsection shows the measurements and tools used in this study, and the third subsection shows the statistical methods adopted in this research.

div.head: Selection of websites
div.p: First, a sample of websites is collected as a case study. The websites of all 27 accredited universities from the Jordanian Higher Education Accreditation Commission (http://www.heac.org.jo/) are selected for this study because of our extensive experience as a faculty member in some of these universities.

Accreditation means implicitly improving the quality of education to all people in the society regardless of whether they are disabled or not. Therefore, universities should consider accessibility and try to offer accessible websites to their visitors. Currently, accredited universities focus on their ranks on the national and international levels, and conduct high-quality research to improve their ranks. Supposedly, accessible websites attract more visitors relative to inaccessible ones. Hence, accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings have to be correlated with one another. Therefore, this study explores the relationships between accessibility and web traffic, accessibility and university rankings, and web traffic and university rankings.

div.head: Evaluation of web accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings
div.p: A number of free online tools are used in this study. The first tool is called WAVE and is used to identify errors (WCAG Violations), alerts, features, structural elements, HTML 5, ARIA, and contrast errors. The second and third tools are AccessMonitor and EIII, which are used to evaluate accessibility. Alexa.com is the fourth tool used to measure the web traffic of different web pages. Webometrics ranking of world universities is used to identify the university rankings of the 27 accredited Jordanian universities under study.

div.head: Statistical methods
div.p: The non-parametric statistical analysis is used to analyse the collected data about 27 Jordanian universities. This study uses Kendall's tau-b and Spearman's rho rank correlations to determine the degree of concordance between two columns of ranked data. The coefficients of these two correlations will decrease as the number of inversions in the two ranks increases. The coefficient range of these two correlations is between -1.0 and 1.0. Generally, Kendall's tau_b obtains better estimations (probabilities) on population parameters relative to Spearman's rho correlation, specifically for a small sample size. Spearman's rho correlation obtains more accurate results than Kendall's tau-b in the case of large discrepancies between two columns of ranked data.

A scale of 1-10 is used by AccessMonitor tool, where 10 represents the optimum (fully accessible URL), and 0 represents the worst (inaccessible URL). All the AccessMonitor (http://www.acessibilidade.gov.pt/accessmonitor/) results are verified; the results are stable and do not fluctuate within the same session as in the EIII Page Checker. This study uses a number of free online tools to assess the accessibility of Jordanian university websites against W3C's WCAG standard. Alexa.com. Subsequently, this study aims to rediscover the relationships between accessibility, web traffic, and university rankings. A fairly strong positive correlation is observed between different accessibility metrics, whereas a fairly weak negative correlation is observed between one of the accessibility metrics and Alexa Ranks; a fairly strong positive correlation is also observed between Alexa Ranks and Webometrics university rankings. Finally, this study explores the difference between the accessibility of public and private Jordanian universities; the statistical analysis using SPSS Mann-Whitney U test shows no difference between the accessibility of private and public Jordanian universities. Future work will explore the use of more metrics and a larger number of universities to assess the relationships between them.
